neighbours.label: A Chinese, Japanese or Korean character that the tokenizer splits into byte pieces, standing alone after a space in English text (e.g. 'wrote 山 in paint') or inside Japanese/Korean prose; peaks on its first byte piece and varies a lot by character. Emoji, chess and math symbols, the euro sign and Cyrillic or Latin letters in the same slot stay low, as does a CJK character glued straight onto an English word.
fire: She wrote 山 in black paint across the top of the scroll.
The sign above the shop door simply read 龍 in faded gold.
My teacher asked me to practice the character 鬱 twenty times.
He tattooed 忍 on his forearm after the trip.
The label on the jar said 塩, which I later learned means salt.
On the map, a small 寺 marked the location of the temple.
Can you tell me how to pronounce 鰻 when ordering at the restaurant?
The stamp at the bottom of the painting showed a single 鶴 in red ink.
quiet: The farmers checked the fences before the storm arrived.
Quantum computing is a much stranger affair, relying instead on the qubit as its unit of information.
She wrote ★ in black paint across the top of the scroll.
The sign above the shop door simply read € in faded gold.
My teacher asked me to practice the symbol ∑ twenty times.
He tattooed ♞ on his forearm after the trip.
The label on the jar said Ж, which I later learned is a Cyrillic letter.
On the map, a small 🏯 marked the location of the temple.
neighbours.notes: Step-in reader of bonsai1/L27/N5995+ (drop 0.50). Card flags the + pole dense (13% of tokens >= 0.1 of max; echo regime). Probes: response varies by character (山 0.54, 風 0.44, 水/火/愛 ~0.18, 한 0.10); plain Japanese/Russian background 0.22-0.32. Test sentences written blind by a label-only author.

predictions: Most fire sentences 0.2-0.6; near misses mostly <0.2, solver leak lines ~0.1-0.2.
